title: Love God, Serve Man -- Ch. 4: On Improving the Administration of Justice

primary_topics: Chapter 4 of 'Love God, Serve Man' -- the extemporaneous report CJP rendered to President Fidel V. Ramos on October 17, 1992 as chairman of the Workshop on Administration of Justice of the Multi-Sectoral Conference, arguing that there can be no peace in the land unless there is first justice that is speedy, efficient and objective.

The workshop's judgment that the government's single-minded pursuit of peace was the major achievement of Ramos's first 100 days (June 30 - October 8, 1992), which CJP hailed as 'the bright dawn of PAX RAMOS in our troubled land of the morning.'

The call for a 'National Covenant of Justice and Peace' binding the President, Congress and most importantly the Supreme Court, with the workshop's written appeal serving as the substitute for a covenant judges are constitutionally barred from signing.

The eleven concrete recommendations for the next 1,000 days -- monitoring of judges and prosecutors, citizen awareness, legal education, police visibility, gun control, and a detailed program for unclogging court dockets -- offered as the means of restoring public confidence in the administration of justice.
sub_topics: The Cenacle opening: the demoralized disciples locked in the upper room after Peter's denial, and the risen Lord's twice-repeated greeting, 'Peace be with you!', as the 2,000-year-old bequest mankind still seeks.
Peace as the theme of the conference and of Ramos's first 100 days, dramatized by the De la Salle choir tearfully singing 'My Peace I Give Unto You' as the invocation.

The governing premise: no genuine peace -- one that solves the root causes of violence rather than merely halting hostilities -- without justice that is speedy, efficient and objective, based on solidarity with the oppressed and meaning development for the poor.

The shared responsibility for the administration of justice: not only the President and Congress but the Supreme Court, vested by the Constitution with administrative supervision over all courts and the power to review grave abuse of discretion.

Appreciation of the Supreme Court's existing measures -- periodic on-the-job training of judges, continuous hearings to resolve cases within 90 days from start of trial, and desk books for judges -- alongside the persisting complaints of serious delay and poor decision quality.

The President's limited role in adjudication: appointing from Judicial and Bar Council nominees, supervising prosecutors through the DOJ and police through the DILG, and reviewing quasi-judicial agency decisions, which he had recently ordered issued within 30 days from submission.

The proposal of a National Covenant of Justice and Peace, and the workshop's written appeal to the President, Chief Justice, Senate President, Speaker and Justice Secretary for bold reforms to hasten prosecution, ensure judicial integrity, improve decisions and expedite enforcement of judgments.

The recommendations sourced from resource speakers former Justice Irene R. Cortes and Dean Eduardo de los Angeles and resource persons Justice Secretary Franklin M. Drilon and Presidential Legal Counsel Antonio T. Carpio: supporting the peace process, a JUDGEWATCH formed by the 188 NGOs, raising citizen awareness, upgrading legal education toward peaceful dispute resolution, and reviving the police 'foot patrol' with barangay Citizens-Police Monitoring Groups.

The docket-unclogging program: small claims courts and summary procedure for claims of P50,000 or less, mandatory arbitration of commercial disputes, relieving the Supreme Court of appeals from the Civil Service Commission and NLRC, strict adherence to constitutional time limits, depositions and discovery, and training judges to mediate settlements at pre-trial.

The remaining proposals -- coordinating the law functions of the DOJ, PCGG and OSG through the Justice Secretary, free legal assistance for indigents, continuing review of legal rules to assure quality decisions free from money, politics and patronage, and review of the adjudication of overseas contract worker cases.
The close: the statistic that more cases are filed than resolved, the paraphrase of John F. Kennedy about negotiating to remove fear, and the benediction returning full circle to the Cenacle.
signature_phrases: the bright dawn of PAX RAMOS in our troubled land of the morning

stances.claim: There can be no genuine peace -- peace that solves the root causes of violence rather than merely halting hostilities -- unless there is first justice that is speedy, efficient and objective, based on solidarity with the oppressed and meaning development for the poor.
stances.rhetorical_move: justice-as-precondition: reversing the usual order by making peace the dependent variable of justice, then defining justice by four cumulative qualities

stances.claim: No real and meaningful judicial reform is possible unless the President, Congress and most importantly the Supreme Court come together in a National Covenant of Justice and Peace; because the Constitution bars justices and judges from non-judicial activity, the workshop addressed a written appeal to all three instead.
stances.rhetorical_move: covenant-and-workaround: proposing a tripartite compact, then conceding the constitutional bar and converting the compact into a public appeal

stances.claim: Despite the Supreme Court's on-the-job training, continuous hearings and desk books, complaints about serious delay and about the quality of decisions persist, and statistics for the past three years show more cases are filed than are resolved, so without the proposed steps justice will be delayed even more.
stances.rhetorical_move: credit-then-critique backed by a filing-versus-disposition statistic

stances.claim: The pursuit of peace will require the leveling of political, social and economic imbalances and therefore sacrifices from all sectors, particularly the affluent and the powerful.
stances.rhetorical_move: cost-naming: attaching an explicit price to the peace process and assigning it to the strong rather than the poor

notable_anecdotes: The Cenacle scene: he opens by placing his audience in the locked upper room with the cowardly, fearful disciples, and notes that the Lord was not satisfied with one greeting but repeated 'Peace be with you!' after showing His pierced hand and slashed side.
The invocation: he recalls the De la Salle choir tearfully singing 'My Peace I Give Unto You' that same morning as the theme of the Multi-Sectoral Conference.
The JUDGEWATCH pledge: the 188 NGOs represented in the conference undertook to form a JUDGEWATCH to monitor the performance and behavior of judges, prosecutors and personnel.

The direct address: mid-speech he turns from exposition to the President himself -- 'And now, Mr. President, let me report to you in summarized form' -- and again at the close, confessing that many are growing weary and even cynical about ever improving the justice system.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 4 of 'Love God, Serve Man' transcribes the extemporaneous report Atty. Artemio V. Panganiban rendered to President Fidel V. Ramos on October 17, 1992 at De La Salle University, Greenhills, as chairman of the Workshop on Administration of Justice of the Multi-Sectoral Conference convened by the Philippine Chamber of Commerce and Industry to propose a program of government for the next 1,000 days. He opened at the Cenacle, where the risen Lord twice greeted the demoralized disciples with 'Peace be with you!', and used that bequest to frame the report: the workshop had chosen the government's single-minded pursuit of peace as the major achievement of Ramos's first 100 days (June 30 to October 8, 1992), seeing 'the bright dawn of PAX RAMOS in our troubled land of the morning.' His premise was that there can be no genuine peace -- one that solves the root causes of violence rather than merely halting hostilities -- without justice first: justice that is speedy, efficient and objective, based on solidarity with the oppressed and meaning development for the poor. He noted the Supreme Court's constitutional powers of administrative supervision and of review for grave abuse of discretion, credited its on-the-job training of judges, continuous hearings within 90 days and desk books, but recorded persisting complaints of delay and of poor decision quality. Because the President's own role in adjudication is limited to appointments, supervision of prosecutors and police, and review of quasi-judicial agencies, he argued that no meaningful reform is possible unless the President, Congress and the Supreme Court join in a 'National Covenant of Justice and Peace'; since judges are barred from non-judicial activity, the workshop instead addressed a written appeal to all three. He then summarized eleven recommendations drawn from resource speakers Irene R. Cortes and Eduardo de los Angeles and resource persons Franklin M. Drilon and Antonio T. Carpio -- supporting the peace process, a JUDGEWATCH formed by 188 NGOs, citizen awareness, upgraded legal education, barangay police visibility and the revived foot patrol, gun control, and docket-unclogging through small claims courts, mandatory commercial arbitration, jurisdictional pruning, strict time limits, discovery and judicial mediation, plus coordination of executive law functions, free legal aid for indigents, continuing review of rules, and review of overseas contract worker cases. Noting that more cases are filed than resolved, he closed by paraphrasing John F. Kennedy -- negotiate to remove fear -- and by invoking the love, justice and peace of Jesus.
